items.headline: Anthropic reverses course and keeps Claude Fable 5 in Max and Team Premium at 50% of limits
items.diff_narrative: Today is a clean turnover: none of yesterday's five substantive storylines carries into today's slate — WAIC survives only as a closing date on the events roll — and the one thread that does reappear arrives inverted. Yesterday Claude Fable 5 showed up purely as a benchmark casualty, with Kimi K3 taking first on the Frontend Code Arena at 1,679 ahead of Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.2, while Anthropic's own slot was Claude Code v2.1.212 shipping agent-safety caps — a changelog story. Today Fable 5 is the subject rather than the comparison point, and the pressure has moved from the leaderboard to the price list: from July 20 the model stays in Max and Team Premium at 50% of limits, Pro and Team Standard get a one-time $100 credit and then API rates, and the underlying weekly limits fall by about a third on the same date, so the 50% allowance applies to a shrinking base. Anthropic named GPT-5.6 Sol as comparable at a fraction of the cost — the vendor conceding on price what yesterday's arena scoreboard implied on capability — and the temporary Claude Code weekly rate-limit boost expires alongside it, which is the same product reappearing as a line in a retrenchment rather than as a feature note.

items.headline: OpenAI discloses GPT-Red, an adversarial self-play red-teamer that beats human red teams 84% to 13%
items.diff_narrative: The security slot keeps its position but changes hands, from measuring the attacker to automating the defender. Yesterday Check Point's report was a field census of offense: AI running exploitation workflows autonomously across dozens of sessions, an 88,000-line command-and-control framework built in under a week, configuration files poisoned so the bypass reloads every session, and longer malicious payloads detected roughly five times more often between March and May. Today OpenAI's GPT-Red is the symmetric move on the other side — an attacker model and a set of diverse defender models trained concurrently by adversarial self-play, reaching an 84% success rate on novel indirect prompt injections against GPT-5.1 where human red teamers managed 13% on identical scenarios, and fully compromising a simulated vending machine across all three objectives. Feeding those attacks back produced the defensive half: six times fewer direct-injection failures in GPT-5.6 Sol than GPT-5.5, a 0.05% failure rate against GPT-Red's own direct injections, above 97% on indirect-injection benchmarks, and fake chain-of-thought attacks falling from north of 95% success to under 10%. The placement is the real difference — yesterday's answer to context-file poisoning was harness-level gating inside a coding agent, today's is hardening baked into the weights and running continuously since GPT-5.3 rather than standing as a pre-launch gate.

items.headline: Walden Robotics leaves stealth with a $300M seed and robots already working inside a Toyota plant
items.diff_narrative: The funding slot moves from late-stage software to seed-stage hardware, and the thing being underwritten changes with it. Yesterday Fireworks AI's $1.5 billion Series D at a $17.5 billion valuation priced an engine that already runs — past $1 billion in annualized revenue, 40 trillion tokens a day, more than 200 models served. Today's raise is roughly a fifth the size at about a sixteenth the valuation and carries no revenue claim at all: Walden Robotics out of stealth with $300 million in seed funding at $1.1 billion, co-led by Toyota and Deviation Capital, built on Russ Tedrake's Large Behavior Models and Diffusion Policy lineage from Toyota Research Institute. What stands in for revenue is a deployment that predates the round — robots doing production work at a Toyota plant in North America since February 2026, first pilot to real tasks in under two months — plus a cap table of prospective customers rather than robotics enthusiasts, with a manufacturer, an aerospace prime, a chip vendor and a warehouse REIT's venture arm sitting together. NVIDIA and Menlo Ventures appear on both days' cap tables, the investor threads that genuinely carry over. The embodied-AI evidence also relocates: yesterday it was 208 embodied-intelligence terminals arranged on a Shanghai exhibition floor, today it is machines on an assembly line.

items.headline: Colibri streams a 744B-parameter mixture-of-experts model off disk to run GLM-5.2 with no GPU
items.diff_narrative: The open-weight slot survives the turnover but changes the question from how large a model can be trained to who can actually execute one. Yesterday Kimi K3 was a 2.8-trillion-parameter sparse mixture-of-experts model activating 16 of 896 experts, an API-first debut at roughly $3 and $15 per million tokens with the weights themselves withheld until July 27 — the scarce thing was access, mediated by an endpoint. Colibri inverts that: a dependency-free C inference engine under Apache 2.0, around 15.9k GitHub stars, treating VRAM, RAM and disk as one managed hierarchy so GLM-5.2's 744 billion parameters run on a machine with about 25GB of RAM and no GPU, keeping roughly 17B of dense layers resident while 19,456 routed experts stream in from a roughly 370GB int4 container on disk under an LRU cache. The scarce thing here is wall-clock time, and the author states the bill plainly — 0.05 to 0.1 tokens per second on a 12-core WSL2 machine, with community reports reaching 1.23 on high-end hardware — batch-job territory rather than interactive chat. Both days are sparse-expert routing stories, but yesterday's was an architecture claim measured on leaderboards and today's is a memory-hierarchy result measured in gigabytes, and GLM-5.2 itself moves from a name Kimi K3 outscored on the Frontend Code Arena to the workload being streamed.

items.headline: Anaconda acquires Kilo Code, folding an agentic coding platform into its enterprise governance stack
items.diff_narrative: The routing-and-serving layer keeps its place in the slate, but the transaction and the pitch both change. Yesterday it was Fireworks AI raising $1.5 billion at a $17.5 billion valuation to serve 40 trillion tokens a day faster across 200-plus models — a capital event underwriting throughput. Today it is Anaconda acquiring Kilo Code on undisclosed terms, consolidation rather than a raise, and the numbers make clear the pitch is not scale: Kilo's roughly 10 trillion tokens a month across more than 3 million developers is about a quarter of what Fireworks moves in a single day, while its gateway routes across 500-plus models spanning open-weight, frontier-cloud and self-hosted endpoints. What is being bought is answerability — agent orchestration paired with package provenance and a policy layer, so an enterprise can see what its coding agents are doing and which models they are calling — with 30-50% token-consumption reductions cited as the payoff, a cost argument landing in the same week as today's Anthropic repricing. Set against yesterday's Claude Code shipping safety caps as a vendor default, the harness market is now consolidating around whoever can satisfy procurement and audit, not only benchmarks.

items.headline: AI events to plan around now: the AGI Summit is underway in San Francisco this weekend
items.diff_narrative: The single genuine continuation, and the clock is what moved. Yesterday the AGI Summit was a weekend to decide on; today it is in progress — July 18-19, 9 AM to 5 PM at the Palace of Fine Arts — and the entry has swapped its speaker-roster pitch for the details that matter once a deadline actually arrives: the street address on Lyon Street, 7 AM doors, $199 general admission and a $49 student rate on a valid .edu address, with the listing source changed as well. WAIC crosses the other way, demoting from yesterday's headline story on the Shanghai show floor to a calendar line noting it closes July 20. Hot Chips gains substance beyond its July 31 early-rate cutoff, with the tutorial program now named — HBM evolution under AI data demand, and RISC-V standards with automotive adoption — drawing Samsung, SK Hynix, NVIDIA and Infineon. AMD's Advancing AI holds its July 22-23 slot but sheds yesterday's expected-silicon detail, and the roll holds its full slate, carrying forward every entry still ahead — the AI Tinkerers meetup in August, the Atlanta leadership summit, the Runway side event the day after DevDay, and NeurIPS in December — alongside the fixed-date anchors. The sequencing advice narrows accordingly: this is now a decision to settle this morning, not one to weigh over the weekend.
